**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Local AI hardware investment decision

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. The case is not that our fleet is adequate — it demonstrably is not at peak times — but that we do not yet know enough about our true demand curve to buy intelligently, and the cheapest way to learn is to fix the scheduling and batching problems we already understand. If utilisation work lifts our effective capacity by even thirty percent, we likely defer a purchase by two quarters; if it does not, we will have spent relatively little and gained precise data about what to buy.

**Where we stand**

Our current cluster runs at roughly forty percent average utilisation, but that average conceals the real problem: weekday afternoons we are saturated, with queued jobs and degraded interactive latency, while nights and weekends the machines sit nearly idle. This is a scheduling failure more than a capacity failure. Long-running training jobs monopolise devices without preemption, batch inference is run at whatever time the owning team finds convenient rather than when capacity exists, and we have no unified queue — teams hoard allocations defensively because they fear losing access, which guarantees the scarcity they fear.

**Cost**

A meaningful hardware expansion would cost on the order of several hundred thousand dollars once you include not just the accelerators but the power, cooling, networking, and rack space, plus the ongoing operational burden. The utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we already employ: building a proper job scheduler with preemption, moving batch workloads into off-peak windows, enabling dynamic batching on the inference services, and instrumenting everything so we can actually see utilisation per job rather than per device. There is a real opportunity cost here too — those engineers could be shipping product features — but the work is bounded, perhaps two to three engineer-quarters, and a portion of it (better observability, a shared queue) pays dividends regardless of what we decide about hardware.

**Latency and reliability**

The counterargument deserves honest treatment. Utilisation improvements do nothing for peak-hour latency if demand genuinely exceeds capacity at those hours; a better scheduler redistributes load, it does not create it. If our interactive services are already missing latency targets at peak, squeezing more throughput onto the same silicon makes that worse, and reliability suffers in ways users feel directly. This is the strongest argument for buying hardware now. But when we examine the peak demand, a large share of it is batch and training work that is latency-tolerant — it simply needs to finish by a deadline. Shifting that load to off-peak hours addresses saturation without touching interactive latency at all. The genuinely latency-sensitive footprint is smaller than the raw queue depth suggests, and we should measure it precisely before concluding that silicon is the constraint.

Reliability also cuts the other way. More hardware means more failure modes, more thermal and power headroom questions, and more maintenance surface for a team that is already stretched thin. Better scheduling, including automatic retry and checkpointing, would improve effective reliability of the jobs we run today — a long training run that survives a node failure is worth more than an idle spare GPU.

**Reversibility**

This is perhaps the decisive consideration. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible: capital is spent, depreciation clocks start, and if demand shifts — a model change reduces our compute needs, or a priority pivot frees capacity — we are stuck with sunk cost and an asset we cannot easily resell at value. Utilisation work is highly reversible. If we build the scheduler and the demand turns out to be genuinely inelastic, we have lost little and can buy with confidence. If we buy first and the demand was partly an artefact of hoarding and poor scheduling, we cannot un-buy.

**Uncertainty**

We should be candid that our demand forecast is weak. We have three months of usable telemetry at best, and growth projections from product are speculative. Buying under this uncertainty means either over-provisioning expensively or under-provisioning and buying again anyway. The utilisation path converts uncertainty into information at low cost.

**Proposed next step**

We propose a ninety-day utilisation programme with explicit success criteria agreed in advance: if peak interactive latency targets are still unmet, or effective capacity gains fall below a threshold we set now, we proceed immediately to a hardware purchase with the data to size it correctly. This is not a way of avoiding the decision — it is a way of making the eventual decision well.

**Internal Memo — From: Platform Engineering — To: Eng Leadership & Infra Team**

**Subject: Buy vs. Utilise — Our Local AI Hardware Decision**

**Date: this week**

**Status: Recommendation attached, decision requested by end of sprint**

---

Team,

We've reached the point where our local inference capacity is being contended for, and we need to decide whether to buy more hardware or get more out of what we already own. I've spent the last two weeks looking at utilisation data, cost projections, and our failure history, and I want to lay out the reasoning before we commit either way. My recommendation, up front, is that we invest in utilisation first — specifically scheduling, batching, and model-serving improvements — and defer the hardware purchase by at least one quarter. Here's why, and where I think I could be wrong.

The cost picture is the most straightforward part. The quote we have for two additional accelerator nodes sits at roughly the annual budget of our entire tooling line, before power, cooling, and the operational overhead of racking and maintaining them. That's not an impossible number, but it's large enough that spending it should require evidence we've exhausted cheaper alternatives. Right now our GPU fleet averages somewhere between 30 and 40 percent utilisation during business hours, with long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. The gap between what we pay for and what we use is the single largest lever available to us, and it costs engineering time rather than capital. Even a modest improvement — getting average utilisation into the 60s — would effectively double our capacity for the price of a few weeks of focused work from two engineers.

Latency is the argument in the other direction, and I want to treat it seriously, because it's the strongest case for buying. Our interactive workloads — the code-assist service and the internal search reranker — have p99 latencies that degrade noticeably when batch jobs queue behind them. More hardware would make that problem disappear immediately. But the latency we're seeing is mostly a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. Jobs are landing on the same nodes as interactive traffic because our scheduler doesn't distinguish between them, and our serving stack doesn't batch small requests intelligently. Fixing that gets us most of the latency win without new metal, and if it doesn't, we'll have learned exactly what we need to size the purchase correctly rather than guessing.

Reliability cuts both ways, and this is where the decision gets genuinely uncomfortable. Our fleet is old enough that we see a hardware failure roughly every six weeks, and each one takes a node out for a day or more. Buying new hardware improves our redundancy margin; a two-node purchase would let us survive a failure without degrading service. Against that, better utilisation means running the existing fleet harder, which will likely accelerate wear and could make failures more frequent in the short term. My honest assessment is that the failure risk is manageable — we have checkpointing on all long-running jobs, and our interactive services already fail over — but I can't promise that with confidence, and we should treat the first month of higher utilisation as a monitored experiment.

The opportunity cost is the part I keep returning to. The engineers who would integrate and commission new hardware are the same people who would build the scheduler and batching improvements, and the utilisation work is the one that compounds: the scheduling layer we build will manage any hardware we eventually buy, so nothing is wasted. The reverse isn't true. If we buy first and utilisation stays poor, we've spent the budget and still own the same software problem.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale — resale value on used accelerators is poor, and the capital is gone. Utilisation work is fully reversible in the sense that if it fails, we've lost time but retained every option, including the purchase we deferred. When one path forecloses options and the other preserves them, and both cost roughly the same in the currency we're shortest of (senior engineering attention), the reversible path should win unless the irreversible one is urgent. I don't believe it is.

What would change my mind: if interactive p99 latency breaches our internal SLO in a way scheduling can't fix, or if utilisation work stalls and we're still contended by mid-quarter, we should buy, and buy quickly rather than deliberating further. I propose we set exactly that trigger now, in writing, so the fallback isn't a debate but a decision.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data with anyone who wants the detail. Please send objections before Thursday's sync.

— Platform Engineering

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Buy more inference hardware, or get more from what we have?
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

---

We've reached the point where our GPU fleet is running hot during business hours and idle at night, and the obvious question on the table is whether we should buy our way out of the squeeze or manage our way out of it. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the two options are not symmetric in cost, risk, or reversibility, and I think the framing matters more than the arithmetic.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our p95 latency on the recommendation model has crept from 180ms to 340ms over the last two quarters, and that degradation tracks almost perfectly with utilisation crossing roughly 75% during peak hours. Queuing theory is unforgiving at that point: small increases in load produce disproportionate increases in wait time, and no amount of clever scheduling fully hides it. Buying capacity would restore headroom immediately, and headroom is what buys us reliability. It also buys us optionality for the two projects queued behind this one, both of which assume inference capacity we don't currently have.

But the purchase case has a cost profile we should look at honestly. At current pricing, the capital outlay for a meaningful increment of capacity is somewhere north of what we spent on the entire original cluster, and the depreciation clock starts the moment the boxes arrive. Hardware in this category has an effective economic life of three to four years before it's competitively obsolete, even if it keeps running longer. That's a real burn rate we're committing to, and it's a commitment made at what may be near the top of a pricing cycle. If accelerator prices soften over the next year, as they have before, we will have bought at the worst possible moment.

The alternative — improving utilisation of what we own — is less glamorous but deserves a fair hearing. Right now, our batch workloads compete with interactive traffic for the same cards, and our overnight window sits largely unused. Time-slicing, better batching of small requests, and moving the training runs to a strict overnight schedule could plausibly recover 20 to 30% of effective capacity. That work costs engineering time, which is the opportunity cost I keep coming back to: every week someone spends on scheduler tuning is a week they're not spending on the features that actually generate revenue. But it's a cost we pay once, roughly, rather than a recurring one, and the skills and tooling we build carry forward to whatever hardware we eventually own.

The decisive consideration for me is reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale. We can't resell enterprise accelerators without taking a significant haircut, and the rack space, power contract, and cooling come along whether we need them or not. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible. If a scheduler change causes problems, we roll it back in an afternoon. If we over-invest in optimisation, we've lost some engineering time and gained tooling we'd want anyway. Asymmetries like that should drive decisions under uncertainty, and we are genuinely uncertain here: our traffic forecast has a wide error band, and the model roadmap could shift demand up or down by a factor of two within six months.

There's also a reliability argument that cuts both ways, and I want to be careful not to oversell the optimisation path. Squeezing utilisation higher means less slack when things fail. A cluster running at 85% has no room to shed load when a node dies; one at 60% absorbs the failure without users noticing. So the goal isn't maximum utilisation — it's *managed* utilisation, with deliberate headroom reserved for failure and burst. That's achievable with what we have, but it requires discipline we haven't yet demonstrated.

My recommendation: defer the purchase for one quarter. Spend that quarter on the utilisation work — overnight scheduling, request batching, and honest measurement of where capacity actually goes — and re-evaluate with real numbers in hand. If, at the end of the quarter, we're still latency-constrained at peak despite genuine effort, the purchase case will be much stronger and better evidenced, and we'll have lost little by waiting. If the optimisation work closes the gap, we'll have saved a very large sum and kept our options open.

I acknowledge the risk in this: deferral means living with degraded latency a bit longer, and if traffic grows faster than forecast, we could end up buying anyway, having spent the quarter's engineering time too. I think that risk is smaller and cheaper than the risk of buying capacity we don't end up needing. But I hold that view with maybe 70% confidence, and I'd genuinely like to hear the counterarguments before we commit.

Happy to walk through the numbers in detail on Thursday.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Buy more GPU hardware, or get more out of what we have?
**Date:** Thursday

We've reached the point in our quarterly planning where the question everyone keeps asking deserves a proper answer: do we spend roughly $180K on two additional GPU nodes, or do we invest the next six to eight weeks in squeezing more out of the four nodes we already own? I've been sitting with this for a while, talking to people on the inference team, the batch jobs side, and finance, and I want to lay out my thinking in full, because the honest answer is more nuanced than either "we need more capacity" or "we're being wasteful."

Let's start with what the data actually says. Our fleet-wide GPU utilisation sits at 41 percent during business hours and drops to 17 percent overnight. That is not a number that screams "buy more iron." A meaningful chunk of our idle capacity comes from scheduling friction: our batch workloads are pinned to specific nodes for historical reasons, our interactive inference traffic is bursty in ways our current queue doesn't smooth, and we have no mechanism for preemption, so a long-running fine-tuning job can block a latency-sensitive request for hours. Before we spend a single dollar on new hardware, we should know what utilisation looks like when those obstacles are removed. My rough modelling suggests better scheduling, dynamic batching on the inference path, and an overnight window for batch work could lift effective utilisation to somewhere in the 60–70 percent range. That is the equivalent of adding two nodes for the cost of engineering time we were mostly going to spend anyway.

That said, utilisation improvements are not free, and I don't want to pretend they are. The engineering effort is real — probably six engineer-weeks across scheduling work, queueing changes, and load testing — and it carries genuine risk. Dynamic batching changes the latency profile of our interactive serving. If we get the batch window or queue depth wrong, p99 latency degrades, and our internal customers will feel it before our dashboards do. There's also a subtler cost: the time we spend on this is time not spent on the model-quality work several of you have been pushing for. Opportunity cost cuts both ways. Buying hardware is fast and boring — order, rack, integrate, done in three weeks — and it frees the team to work on things closer to the product. Improving utilisation is slower and more interesting, but it consumes exactly the attention we're always short of.

On reliability, the picture favours caution about buying. Our current nodes have a mean time between failures that's acceptable but not great, and adding two more nodes adds two more things that fail, two more driver stacks to maintain, and more surface area for the thermal and networking issues we've already chased this year. Better utilisation of existing hardware doesn't add failure modes; it mostly adds software complexity, which we can test, stage, and roll back. That last point matters more than it might first appear. This decision is fundamentally about reversibility. Hardware is a one-way door in practice: capital is committed, depreciation starts, and if demand shifts — say, a model change lets us serve the same traffic on smaller models, or a vendor API becomes good enough that we offload a workload — we're stuck carrying capacity we no longer need. Software changes to scheduling and batching are a revolving door. If dynamic batching turns out to hurt latency in ways we didn't anticipate, we revert in an afternoon.

So where does the uncertainty lie? Mostly in demand. Our traffic forecasts have been wrong in both directions this year, and if the new internal customer onboarding in Q3 lands the way their team projects, our peak-hour headroom shrinks to something uncomfortable even with improved utilisation. I don't want to optimise so hard that we have no slack for a genuine spike, because the cost of turning away work — or of serving it late — is higher than the cost of idle GPUs at 3 a.m.

My recommendation, then: commit now to the utilisation work, with a concrete target of 60 percent effective utilisation by the end of next quarter, and treat the hardware purchase as a contingent decision we revisit with better data rather than a choice we must make today. If utilisation improvements stall, or Q3 demand materialises as forecast, we buy one node rather than two and revisit again. This sequencing costs us a few weeks of potential headroom, which I judge a fair price for making an expensive, hard-to-reverse decision with evidence instead of anxiety. I'd like to align on this at Monday's planning session — please come with objections, especially from those of you closest to the serving path.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've reached the point in the quarter where the question we've been deferring can no longer be deferred: do we spend roughly $180K on two additional GPU nodes, or do we invest the next six weeks in squeezing more out of the four nodes we already own? I've been sitting with this for a while, and I want to lay out my thinking in full, because the honest answer is more nuanced than either "we need more hardware" or "we're just being wasteful."

Let's start with what the data actually says. Our fleet-wide utilisation sits at 41% during business hours and drops to 12% overnight. That number is genuinely alarming on its face, and if I only looked at it, I'd conclude we have no business buying anything. But averages hide the shape of the problem. Our peak concurrent demand — the Thursday afternoon training runs plus the inference traffic that serves the internal search product — pushes three of our four nodes to 95% or higher for stretches of two to three hours. The queueing during those windows is real: experiment turnaround time degrades from twenty minutes to sometimes ninety, and that latency hits the team where it hurts most, in iteration velocity. Researchers who wait an hour and a half for a result start batching their questions conservatively, running fewer, safer experiments. That's an invisible tax on the quality of our work, and it doesn't show up in any utilisation dashboard.

So the picture is simultaneously "we have plenty of idle capacity" and "we are capacity-starved at the moments that matter." The question is which problem is cheaper to fix.

The case for better utilisation is strong and I want to argue it sincerely rather than as a token concession. Most of our overnight idleness is a scheduling failure, not a physical constraint. Our training jobs are manually launched, our inference capacity is statically partitioned per service, and nobody has built the queueing layer that would let a batch job soak up spare cycles at 2 a.m. A competent scheduler — whether we build one on top of open-source tooling or adopt something off the shelf — could plausibly lift average utilisation from 41% to 65% or better. That's the equivalent of adding roughly one and a half nodes for the cost of maybe six engineer-weeks. On pure dollars-per-flops, that's an order of magnitude better than buying hardware, and unlike hardware, it doesn't consume rack space, power, or our already-strained cooling budget.

But utilisation improvements have a ceiling, and it's important to be honest about where that ceiling is. Scheduling can fix the valleys; it cannot fix the peaks. If Thursday afternoons genuinely require five nodes' worth of compute, no amount of clever overnight packing changes that. We can shift some batch workloads in time, and we should, but interactive inference latency is not deferrable — the search product needs its responses in milliseconds, and the researchers need their Thursday slots. There's also a reliability dimension here that I take seriously: right now, the loss of a single node takes a third of our fleet offline, and our inference serving has no meaningful redundancy. Two more nodes would let us survive a hardware failure without customer-visible degradation. A scheduler, however good, does nothing for fault tolerance.

Which brings me to opportunity cost and reversibility, the two lenses I think should actually decide this. Six engineer-weeks spent on scheduling is six weeks not spent on the product roadmap, and that's a real cost — but it's a cost we can stop paying at any time. A scheduling project that stalls can be abandoned with nothing lost but time. Hardware, by contrast, is a one-way door in practical terms: once purchased, it depreciates whether we use it or not, it locks us into a power and cooling commitment, and if our model mix shifts toward workloads that don't fit this hardware class, we can't easily resell our way out. The asymmetry favours doing the reversible thing first.

My recommendation, then: we do both, but in sequence, not in parallel. We commit the next six weeks to the scheduling and partitioning work, with a concrete target — peak-hour queue wait under fifteen minutes and average utilisation above 60%. If we hit that target and the Thursday peaks still hurt, we buy one node, not two, in the next budget cycle, and we revisit redundancy separately, possibly through a cloud burst arrangement rather than owned hardware.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My 65% utilisation estimate is informed guesswork, not measurement; if the real ceiling is 50%, the case for buying weakens only slightly, but the case for hiring or reprioritising strengthens. And demand itself is a moving target — if the search product grows the way the product team projects, today's peak becomes next quarter's baseline and the purchase question returns with force.

I'd like to align on this in Friday's sync. The scheduler work is the right first move: cheap, reversible, and it makes whatever we eventually buy smaller and better justified.
